**Mary Stevenson Cassatt** ([/k ə ˈ s æ t/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); May 22, 1844–June 14, 1926)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-1) was an American [painter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Painter "Painter") and [printmaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printmaker "Printmaker").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-NYT-20240516-2) She was born in [Allegheny, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegheny,_Pennsylvania "Allegheny, Pennsylvania") (now part of [Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh "Pittsburgh")'s [North Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Side_(Pittsburgh) "North Side (Pittsburgh)")), but lived most of her adult life in France, where she befriended [Edgar Degas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Degas "Edgar Degas") and exhibited with the [Impressionists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impressionists "Impressionists"). Cassatt often created images of the social and private lives of women, with particular emphasis on the intimate bonds between mothers and children.

She was described by [Gustave Geffroy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustave_Geffroy "Gustave Geffroy") as one of "les trois grandes dames" (the three great ladies) of Impressionism alongside [Marie Bracquemond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Bracquemond "Marie Bracquemond") and [Berthe Morisot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berthe_Morisot "Berthe Morisot").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-3) In 1879, Diego Martelli compared her to Degas, as they both sought to depict movement, light, and design in the most modern sense.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-4) She also played an important role in introducing Impressionism to American collectors, notably through her friendship with the [Havemeyer family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Havemeyer_family "Havemeyer family").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-5)

Cassatt was born in [Allegheny, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegheny,_Pennsylvania "Allegheny, Pennsylvania"), which is now part of [Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh "Pittsburgh").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-Columbus_Museum_of_Art_p.36-6) She was born into an [upper-middle-class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_middle_class "Upper middle class") family:[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollock1998280-7) Her father, Robert Simpson Cassat (later Cassatt), was a successful stockbroker and land speculator. The ancestral name had been Cossart, with the family descended from French [Huguenot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huguenot "Huguenot") Jacques Cossart, who came to [New Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Amsterdam "New Amsterdam") in 1662.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews19983-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-americanwoman-9) Her mother, Katherine Kelso Johnston, came from a banking family. Katherine Cassatt, educated and well-read, had a profound influence on her daughter.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollock1998281%E2%80%9382-10) To that effect, Cassatt's lifelong friend [Louisine Havemeyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisine_Havemeyer "Louisine Havemeyer") wrote in her memoirs: "Anyone who had the privilege of knowing Mary Cassatt's mother would know at once that it was from her and her alone that [Mary] inherited her ability."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-11) A distant cousin of artist [Robert Henri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Henri "Robert Henri"),[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-12) Cassatt was one of seven children, of whom two died in infancy. One brother, [Alexander Johnston Cassatt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Cassatt "Alexander Cassatt"), later became president of the [Pennsylvania Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Railroad "Pennsylvania Railroad"). The family moved eastward, first to [Lancaster, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancaster,_Pennsylvania "Lancaster, Pennsylvania"), then to the [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia") area, where she started her schooling at the age of six.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-:1-13)

Cassatt grew up in an environment that viewed travel as an integral part of a well-rounded education. She spent five years in Europe and visited many of the capitals, including London, Paris, and Berlin. While abroad, she learned German and French and had her first lessons in drawing and music.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews199811-14) It is likely that her first exposure to French artists [Jean Auguste Dominique Ingres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Auguste_Dominique_Ingres "Jean Auguste Dominique Ingres"), [Eugène Delacroix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eug%C3%A8ne_Delacroix "Eugène Delacroix"), [Camille Corot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Baptiste-Camille_Corot "Jean-Baptiste-Camille Corot"), and [Gustave Courbet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustave_Courbet "Gustave Courbet") was at the [Paris World's Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_World's_Fair "Paris World's Fair") of 1855. Also in the exhibition were [Edgar Degas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Degas "Edgar Degas") and [Camille Pissarro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camille_Pissarro "Camille Pissarro"), both of whom were later her colleagues and mentors.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKown197210%E2%80%9312-15)

Though her family objected to her becoming a professional artist, Cassatt began studying painting at the [Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Academy_of_the_Fine_Arts "Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts") in Philadelphia at the early age of 15.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews199815-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-Presutti%E2%80%932024-17) Part of her parents' concern may have been Cassatt's exposure to [feminist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feminism "Feminism") ideas and the bohemian behavior of some of the male students. Cassatt and her network of friends became lifelong advocates of [equal rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equal_rights_for_women "Equal rights for women") for the sexes.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-:0-18) Although about 20% of the students were female, most viewed art as a socially valuable skill. Few of them were determined, as Cassatt was, to make art their career.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews199418-19) She continued her studies from 1861 through 1865, during the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-Columbus_Museum_of_Art_p.36-6)[Thomas Eakins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Eakins "Thomas Eakins") was among her fellow students; he was later forced to resign as director of the academy.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-:1-13)

Impatient with the slow pace of instruction and the patronizing attitude of the male students and teachers, she decided to study the [old masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Master "Old Master") on her own. She later said: "There was no teaching" at the academy. Female students could not use live models until somewhat later, and the principal training was primarily drawing from casts.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKown197216-20)

Cassatt decided to end her studies. At that time, no degree was granted. After overcoming her father's objections, she moved to Paris in 1866, with her mother and family friends acting as [chaperones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaperone_(social) "Chaperone (social)").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews199429-21) Since women could not yet attend the [École des Beaux-Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89cole_des_Beaux-Arts "École des Beaux-Arts"), Cassatt applied to study privately with masters from the school[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews199431-22) and was accepted to study with [Jean-Léon Gérôme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-L%C3%A9on_G%C3%A9r%C3%B4me "Jean-Léon Gérôme"), a highly regarded teacher known for his hyper-realistic technique and his depiction of exotic subjects. (A few months later, Gérôme also accepted Eakins as a student.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews199431-22)) Cassatt augmented her artistic training with daily copying in the [Louvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louvre "Louvre"), obtaining the required permit, which was necessary to control the "copyists", usually low-paid women, who daily filled the museum to paint copies for sale. The museum also served as a social place for Frenchmen and American female students, who, like Cassatt, were not allowed to attend [cafes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffeehouse "Coffeehouse") where the avant-garde socialized. In this manner, fellow artist and friend [Elizabeth Jane Gardner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Jane_Gardner "Elizabeth Jane Gardner") met and married famed academic painter [William-Adolphe Bouguereau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William-Adolphe_Bouguereau "William-Adolphe Bouguereau").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews199432-23)

_[The Boating Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Boating\_Party "The Boating Party")_ by Mary Cassatt, 1893–94, oil on canvas, 35½ × 46 in., [National Gallery of Art, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Gallery_of_Art,_Washington "National Gallery of Art, Washington")

Toward the end of 1866, she joined a painting class taught by [Charles Joshua Chaplin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Joshua_Chaplin "Charles Joshua Chaplin"), a [genre artist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genre_art "Genre art"). In 1868, Cassatt also studied with artist [Thomas Couture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Couture "Thomas Couture"), whose subjects were mostly romantic and urban.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews199454-24) On trips to the countryside, the students drew from life, particularly the peasants going about their daily activities. In 1868, one of her paintings, _A Mandoline Player_, was accepted for the first time by the selection jury for the [Paris Salon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Salon "Paris Salon"). With [Elizabeth Jane Gardner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Jane_Gardner "Elizabeth Jane Gardner"), whose work was also accepted by the jury that year, Cassatt was one of two American women to first exhibit in the Salon.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-americanwoman-9)_A Mandoline Player_ is in the [Romantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanticism "Romanticism") style of [Corot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Baptiste-Camille_Corot "Jean-Baptiste-Camille Corot") and Couture,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews199847-25) and is one of only two paintings from the first decade of her career that is documented today.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews199854-26)

The French art scene was in a process of change, as radical artists such as Courbet and [Édouard Manet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89douard_Manet "Édouard Manet") tried to break away from accepted Academic tradition, and the Impressionists were in their formative years. Cassatt's friend Eliza Haldeman wrote home that artists "are leaving the Academy style and each seeking a new way, consequently just now everything is Chaos."[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews199432-23) Cassatt, on the other hand, continued to work in the traditional manner, submitting works to the Salon for over ten years, with increasing frustration.

Returning to the United States in the late summer of 1870—as the [Franco-Prussian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franco-Prussian_War "Franco-Prussian War") was starting[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-Presutti%E2%80%932024-17)—Cassatt lived with her family in [Altoona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altoona,_Pennsylvania "Altoona, Pennsylvania"). Her father continued to resist her chosen vocation, paying for her basic needs but not her art supplies.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews199875-27) Cassatt placed two of her paintings in a New York gallery and found many admirers but no purchasers. She was also dismayed at the lack of paintings to study while staying at her summer residence. Cassatt even considered giving up art, as she was determined to make a living independently. She wrote in a letter of July 1871, "I have given up my studio & torn up my father's portrait, & have not touched a brush for six weeks nor ever will again until I see some prospect of getting back to Europe. I am very anxious to go out west next fall & get some employment, but I have not yet decided where."[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews199474-28)

Cassatt traveled to Chicago to try her luck, but lost some of her early paintings in the [Great Chicago Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire "Great Chicago Fire") of 1871.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKown197236-29) Shortly afterward, her work attracted the attention of Roman Catholic Bishop [Michael Domenec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Domenec "Michael Domenec") of Pittsburgh, who commissioned her to paint two copies of paintings by [Correggio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Correggio "Correggio") in [Parma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parma "Parma"), Italy, advancing her enough money to cover her travel expenses and part of her stay.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-30) In her excitement she wrote, "O how wild I am to get to work, my fingers farely itch & my eyes water to see a fine picture again".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews199476-31) With [Emily Sartain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emily_Sartain "Emily Sartain"), a fellow artist from a well-regarded artistic family from Philadelphia, Cassatt set out for Europe again.

## Impressionism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mary_Cassatt&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Impressionism")]

Within months of her return to Europe in the autumn of 1871, Cassatt's prospects had brightened. Her painting _Two Women Throwing Flowers During Carnival_ was well received in the Salon of 1872 and was purchased. She attracted much favorable notice in Parma and was supported and encouraged by the art community there: "All Parma is talking of Miss Cassatt and her picture, and everyone is anxious to know her".[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews199479-32)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/48/Mary_Cassatt_-_Portrait_of_Mrs._Currey%3B_Sketch_of_Mr._Cassatt.jpg/250px-Mary_Cassatt_-_Portrait_of_Mrs._Currey%3B_Sketch_of_Mr._Cassatt.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mary_Cassatt_-_Portrait_of_Mrs._Currey;_Sketch_of_Mr._Cassatt.jpg)

Oil, c.1871, private collection. Mrs. Currey had worked for the Cassatt family. When Mary Cassatt returned home from Paris at the outbreak of the Franco-Prussian War, she asked Mrs. Currey to pose for her and gave her the sketch. Superimposed (the canvas turned upside down) is a sketch of her father.

After completing her commission for the bishop, Cassatt traveled to [Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madrid "Madrid") and [Seville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville "Seville"), where she painted a group of paintings of Spanish subjects, including _Spanish Dancer Wearing a Lace Mantilla_ (1873, in the [National Museum of American Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_Art "National Museum of American Art"), [Smithsonian Institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution")). In 1874, she made the decision to take up residence in France. She was joined by her sister, Lydia, who shared an apartment with her. Cassatt opened a studio in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris"). [Louisa May Alcott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisa_May_Alcott "Louisa May Alcott")'s sister, [Abigail May Alcott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abigail_May_Alcott_Nieriker "Abigail May Alcott Nieriker"), was then an art student in Paris and visited Cassatt.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-americanwoman-9) Cassatt continued to express criticism of the politics of the Salon and the conventional taste that prevailed there. She was blunt in her comments, as reported by Sartain, who wrote: "she is entirely too slashing, snubs all modern art, disdains the Salon pictures of [Cabanel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandre_Cabanel "Alexandre Cabanel"), [Bonnat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9on_Bonnat "Léon Bonnat"), all the names we are used to revere".[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews199487-33)

Cassatt saw that works by female artists were often dismissed with contempt unless the artist had a friend or protector on the jury, and she would not flirt with jurors to curry favor.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews1998104%E2%80%93105-34) Her cynicism grew when one of the two pictures she submitted in 1875 was refused by the jury, only to be accepted the following year after she darkened the background. She had quarrels with Sartain, who thought Cassatt too outspoken and self-centered, and eventually they parted. Out of her distress and self-criticism, Cassatt decided that she needed to move away from genre paintings and onto more fashionable subjects, in order to attract portrait commissions from American socialites abroad, but that attempt bore little fruit at first.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews199496-35)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/32/Mary_CASSATT%2C_Portrait_de_fillette.JPG/250px-Mary_CASSATT%2C_Portrait_de_fillette.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mary_CASSATT,_Portrait_de_fillette.JPG)

_Portrait de fillette_, 1879, [Musée des Beaux-Arts de Bordeaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_des_Beaux-Arts_de_Bordeaux "Musée des Beaux-Arts de Bordeaux")

In 1877, both her entries were rejected, and for the first time in seven years, she had no works in the Salon.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews1998100-36) At this low point in her career, she was invited by Edgar Degas to show her works with the [Impressionists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impressionism "Impressionism"), a group that had begun their own series of independent exhibitions in 1874 with much attendant notoriety. The Impressionists (also known as the "Independents" or "Intransigents") had no formal manifesto and varied considerably in subject matter and technique. They tended to prefer [plein air](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plein_air "Plein air") painting and the application of vibrant color in separate strokes with little pre-mixing, which allows the eye to merge the results in an "impressionistic" manner. The Impressionists had been receiving the wrath of the critics for several years. Henry Bacon, a friend of the Cassatts, thought that the Impressionists were so radical that they were "afflicted with some hitherto unknown disease of the eye".[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews1994107-37) They already had one female member, artist [Berthe Morisot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berthe_Morisot "Berthe Morisot"), who became Cassatt's friend and colleague. The only American officially associated with the Impressionists, Cassatt would go on to exhibit in half of the group's later exhibitions[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-38)

Cassatt admired Degas, whose [pastels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pastel "Pastel") had made a powerful impression on her when she encountered them in an art dealer's window in 1875. "I used to go and flatten my nose against that window and absorb all I could of his art," she later recalled. "It changed my life. I saw art then as I wanted to see it."[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews1998114-39) She accepted Degas' invitation with enthusiasm and began preparing paintings for the next Impressionist show, planned for 1878, which (after a postponement because of the World's Fair) took place on April 10, 1879. She felt comfortable with the Impressionists and joined their cause enthusiastically, declaring: "we are carrying on a despairing fight & need all our forces".[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews1994118-40) Unable to attend cafes with them without attracting unfavorable attention, she met with them privately and at exhibitions. She now hoped for commercial success selling paintings to the sophisticated Parisians who preferred the avant-garde. Her style had gained a new spontaneity during the intervening two years. Previously a studio-bound artist, she had adopted the practice of carrying a sketchbook with her while out-of-doors or at the theater, and recording the scenes she saw.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews1994125-41)

_Summertime_ by Mary Cassatt, c.1894, oil on canvas, [Terra Foundation for American Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terra_Foundation_for_American_Art "Terra Foundation for American Art"), [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago")

In 1877, Cassatt was joined in Paris by her father and mother, who returned with her sister Lydia, all eventually to share a large apartment on the fifth floor of 13, Avenue Trudaine. Mary valued their companionship, as neither she nor Lydia had married. A case was made that Mary had narcissistic disturbance, never completing the recognition of herself as a person outside of the orbit of her mother.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-42) Mary had decided early in life that marriage would be incompatible with her career. Lydia, who was frequently painted by her sister, had recurrent bouts of illness, and her death in 1882 left Cassatt temporarily unable to work.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews1998163-43)

Cassatt's father insisted that her studio and supplies be covered by her sales, which were still meager. Afraid of having to paint "[potboilers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potboiler "Potboiler")" to make ends meet, Cassatt applied herself to produce some quality paintings for the next Impressionist exhibition.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-:1-13) Three of her most accomplished works from 1878 were _Portrait of the Artist_ (self-portrait), _[Little Girl in a Blue Armchair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little\_Girl\_in\_a\_Blue\_Armchair "Little Girl in a Blue Armchair")_, and _Reading Le Figaro_ (portrait of her mother).

Mary Cassatt, _Woman Standing Holding a Fan_, 1878–79, ([Amon Carter Museum of American Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amon_Carter_Museum_of_American_Art "Amon Carter Museum of American Art"))

Degas had considerable influence on Cassatt. Both were highly experimental in their use of materials, trying [distemper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distemper_(paint) "Distemper (paint)") and metallic paints in many works, such as _Woman Standing Holding a Fan_, 1878–79 ([Amon Carter Museum of American Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amon_Carter_Museum_of_American_Art "Amon Carter Museum of American Art")).[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-44)

She became extremely proficient in the use of [pastels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pastel "Pastel"), eventually creating many of her most important works in this medium. Degas also introduced her to [etching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etching "Etching"), of which he was a recognized master. The two worked side by side for a while, and her [draftsmanship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drawing "Drawing") gained considerable strength under his tutelage. One example of her thoughtful approach to the medium of drypoint as a mode for reflecting on her status as an artist is 'Reflection' of 1889–90, which has recently been interpreted as a self-portrait.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-45) Degas in turn depicted Cassatt in a series of etchings recording their trips to the Louvre. She treasured his friendship but learned not to expect too much from his fickle and temperamental nature after a project they were collaborating on at the time, a proposed journal devoted to prints, was abruptly dropped by him.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews1994146%E2%80%9350-46) The sophisticated and well-dressed Degas, then forty-five, was a welcome dinner guest at the Cassatt residence, and likewise they at his _soirées_.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews1994128%E2%80%9331,_147-47)

The Impressionist exhibit of 1879 was the most successful to date, despite the absence of [Renoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre-Auguste_Renoir "Pierre-Auguste Renoir"), [Sisley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Sisley "Alfred Sisley"), [Manet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89douard_Manet "Édouard Manet") and [Cézanne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_C%C3%A9zanne "Paul Cézanne"), who were attempting once again to gain recognition at the Salon. Through the efforts of [Gustave Caillebotte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustave_Caillebotte "Gustave Caillebotte"), who organized and underwrote the show, the group made a profit and sold many works, although the criticism continued as harsh as ever. The _Revue des Deux Mondes_ wrote, "M. Degas and Mlle. Cassatt are, nevertheless, the only artists who distinguish themselves... and who offer some attraction and some excuse in the pretentious show of window dressing and infantile daubing".[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKown197273-48)

Cassatt displayed eleven works, including _Lydia in a Loge, Wearing a Pearl Necklace, (Woman in a Loge)_. Although critics claimed that Cassatt's colors were too bright and that her portraits were too accurate to be flattering to the subjects, her work was not savaged as was [Monet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Monet "Claude Monet")'s, whose circumstances were the most desperate of all the Impressionists at that time. She used her share of the profits to purchase a work by Degas and one by Monet.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKown197272%E2%80%9373-49) She participated in the Impressionist Exhibitions that followed in 1880 and 1881, and she remained an active member of the Impressionist circle until 1886. In 1886, Cassatt provided two paintings for the first Impressionist exhibition in the US, organized by art dealer [Paul Durand-Ruel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Durand-Ruel "Paul Durand-Ruel"). Her friend [Louisine Elder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisine_Elder "Louisine Elder") married [Harry Havemeyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H.O._Havemeyer "H.O. Havemeyer") in 1883, and with Cassatt as advisor, the couple began collecting the Impressionists on a grand scale. Much of their vast collection is now in the [Metropolitan Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Museum_of_Art "Metropolitan Museum of Art") in New York City.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews1994167-50)

Cassatt also made several portraits of family members during that period, of which _Portrait of Alexander Cassatt and His Son Robert Kelso_ (1885) is one of her best-regarded. Cassatt's style then evolved, and she moved away from Impressionism to a simpler, more straightforward approach. She began to exhibit her works in New York galleries as well. After 1886, Cassatt no longer identified herself with any art movement and experimented with a variety of techniques.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-:1-13)

## Feminist viewpoints and the "New Woman"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mary_Cassatt&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Feminist viewpoints and the \"New Woman\"")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/Mary_Cassatt%2C_Reading_%E2%80%9CLe_Figaro%E2%80%9D%2C_1878%2C_Collection_Mrs._Eric_de_Spoelberch%2C_Haverford%2C_Pennsylvania.jpg/250px-Mary_Cassatt%2C_Reading_%E2%80%9CLe_Figaro%E2%80%9D%2C_1878%2C_Collection_Mrs._Eric_de_Spoelberch%2C_Haverford%2C_Pennsylvania.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mary_Cassatt,_Reading_%E2%80%9CLe_Figaro%E2%80%9D,_1878,_Collection_Mrs._Eric_de_Spoelberch,_Haverford,_Pennsylvania.jpg)

_Reading "Le Figaro"_ by Mary Cassatt (1878), Collection Mrs. Eric de Spoelberch, Haverford, Pennsylvania

Cassatt and her contemporaries enjoyed the wave of feminism that occurred in the 1840s, allowing them access to educational institutions at newly coed colleges and universities, such as [Oberlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oberlin_College "Oberlin College") and the [University of Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Michigan "University of Michigan"). Likewise, women's colleges such as [Vassar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vassar_College "Vassar College"), [Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smith_College "Smith College") and [Wellesley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wellesley_College "Wellesley College") opened their doors during this time. Cassatt was an outspoken advocate for [women's equality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_equality "Women's equality"), campaigning with her friends for equal travel scholarships for students in the 1860s, and the [right to vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suffrage "Suffrage") in the 1910s.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-:0-18)

Mary Cassatt depicted the "[New Woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Woman "New Woman")" of the 19th century from the woman's perspective. As a successful, highly trained woman artist who never married, Cassatt—like [Ellen Day Hale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellen_Day_Hale "Ellen Day Hale"), [Elizabeth Coffin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Coffin "Elizabeth Coffin"), [Elizabeth Nourse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Nourse "Elizabeth Nourse") and [Cecilia Beaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecilia_Beaux "Cecilia Beaux")—personified the "New Woman".[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-51) She "initiated the profound beginnings in recreating the image of the 'new' woman", drawn from the influence of her intelligent and active mother, Katherine Cassatt, who believed in educating women to be knowledgeable and socially active. She is depicted in _Reading 'Le Figaro'_(1878).[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-52)

Cassatt's independence and choice not to marry as a "New Woman" could also be seen as a reaction to the strict institutionalized misogamy of the art world at the time, in which a woman artist's marriage could have been seen as incompatible with any serious artistic career.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-thecrimson.com-53)

Although Cassatt did not explicitly make political statements about women's rights in her work, her artistic portrayal of women was consistently done with dignity and the suggestion of a deeper, meaningful inner life.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-:0-18) Many of her works depict a mother caring for a child and she painted them with warmth and attention.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-54) Unlike the other Impressionists of the time who often painted street scenes and landscapes, Cassatt preferred to depict the everyday life of women and the domestic labors associated with the home.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-halifaxpubliclibraries.ca-55) This was unusual at the time because, while Impressionist pieces typically depicted women as passive objects for the viewer, Cassatt notably made the women she painted active observers with real engagement in their environments. Cassatt's work was shaped by her time spent engaging with these women in their private, intimate spaces, something that a male artist would not have had the social ability to do at that time.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-thecrimson.com-53) This disconnect from what the two different genders were allowed to observe as artists did not go unnoticed by Cassatt, and she notably enjoyed observing the complexities of gender relations in her work. The piece _In the Loge_ (1878) is a good example of this, as it depicts a young woman watching the opera while a male admirer gawks at her from afar. The viewer is then also included in the voyeuristic objectification of the unaware model, exposing the social dynamics of the time.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-56)

By choosing to depict more humble feminine environments Cassatt effectively raised scenes of women, their labor, friendships, and personal life to be celebrated as high art.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-57) She was often critiqued for this preference and her art dismissed as too feminine.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-halifaxpubliclibraries.ca-55) Cassatt objected to being stereotyped as a "woman artist"; she supported [women's suffrage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage "Women's suffrage") and, in 1915, showed eighteen works in an exhibition supporting the movement organised by Louisine Havemeyer, a committed and active feminist.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-HyperA-58) The exhibition brought her into conflict with her sister-in-law [Eugenie Carter Cassatt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gardner_(Cassatt)_Held_by_His_Mother "Gardner (Cassatt) Held by His Mother"), who was [anti-suffrage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-suffragism "Anti-suffragism") and who boycotted the show along with Philadelphia society in general. Cassatt responded by selling off her work that was otherwise destined for her heirs. In particular _[The Boating Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Boating\_Party "The Boating Party")_, thought to have been inspired by the birth of Eugenie's daughter Ellen Mary, was bought by the National Gallery, Washington, D.C.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews1994306%E2%80%9310-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-60)

## Relationship with Degas

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mary_Cassatt&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Relationship with Degas")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/35/Mary_Stevenson_Cassatt.jpg/250px-Mary_Stevenson_Cassatt.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mary_Stevenson_Cassatt.jpg)

Edgar Degas, _Mary Cassatt Seated, Holding Cards_, c.1880–1884, oil on canvas, 74 × 60 cm, [National Portrait Gallery, Washington DC. NPG.84.34](http://npgportraits.si.edu/emuseumCAP/code/emuseum.asp) Cassatt hated it later and wrote to her dealer Paul Durand-Ruel in 1912 or 1913 that "I don't want anyone to know that I posed for it."

Cassatt and Degas had a long period of collaboration. The two painters had studios close together, Cassatt at 19, rue Laval, Degas at 4, rue Frochot,[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarter1998354%E2%80%93355_%22Mary_Cassatt's_Paris%22_(map)-61) less than a five-minute walk apart, and Degas developed the habit of looking in at Cassatt's studio and offering her advice and helping her gain models.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews1994125-41)

They had much in common: they shared similar tastes in art and literature, came from affluent backgrounds, had studied painting in Italy, and both were independent, never marrying. The degree of intimacy between them cannot be assessed now, as no letters survive, but it is unlikely they were in a sexual relationship, given their conservative social backgrounds and strong adherence to the prevalent notions of sexual morality at the time.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Several of [Vincent van Gogh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_van_Gogh "Vincent van Gogh")'s letters attest to Degas' sexual self-constraint.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-62)[_[non-primary source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:No\_original\_research#Primary,\_secondary\_and\_tertiary\_sources "Wikipedia:No original research")_] Degas introduced Cassatt to pastel and engraving, both of which Cassatt quickly mastered, while for her part, Cassatt was instrumental in helping Degas sell his paintings and promoting his reputation in America.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBullard14-63)

Both regarded themselves as figure painters, and the art historian George Shackelford suggests they were influenced by the art critic [Louis Edmond Duranty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Edmond_Duranty "Louis Edmond Duranty")'s appeal in his pamphlet _The New Painting_ for a revitalization in figure painting: "Let us take leave of the stylized human body, which is treated like a vase. What we need is the characteristic modern person in his clothes, in the midst of his social surroundings, at home or out in the street."[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDuranty1876-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-65)

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/Mary_Stevenson_Cassatt_-_Mary_Cassatt_Self-Portrait_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg/250px-Mary_Stevenson_Cassatt_-_Mary_Cassatt_Self-Portrait_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mary_Stevenson_Cassatt_-_Mary_Cassatt_Self-Portrait_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg)

Mary Cassatt, _Self-Portrait_, c.1880, gouache and watercolor over graphite on paper, 32.7 cm × 24.6 cm, National Portrait Gallery, Washington, D.C. NPG.76.33[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-66)

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9c/Cassat_-_Blue_Armchair_NGA.jpg/250px-Cassat_-_Blue_Armchair_NGA.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cassat_-_Blue_Armchair_NGA.jpg)

_[Little Girl in a Blue Armchair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little\_Girl\_in\_a\_Blue\_Armchair "Little Girl in a Blue Armchair")_, 1878

After Cassatt's parents and sister, Lydia, joined Cassatt in Paris in 1877, Degas, Cassatt, and Lydia were often to be seen at the Louvre studying artworks together. Degas produced two prints, notable for their technical innovation, depicting Cassatt at the Louvre looking at artworks while Lydia reads a guidebook. These were destined for a prints journal planned by Degas (together with [Camille Pissarro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camille_Pissarro "Camille Pissarro") and others), which never came to fruition. Cassatt frequently posed for Degas, notably for his millinery series trying on hats.

Around 1884, Degas made a portrait in oils of Cassatt, _Mary Cassatt Seated, Holding Cards_.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-68) A _Self-Portrait_ (c.1880) by Cassatt depicts her in the identical hat and dress, leading art historian [Griselda Pollock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Griselda_Pollock "Griselda Pollock") to speculate they were executed in a joint painting session in the early years of their acquaintance.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollock1998118-69)

Cassatt and Degas worked most closely together in the fall and winter of 1879–80, when Cassatt was mastering her printmaking technique. Degas owned a small printing press, and by day she worked at his studio using his tools and press while in the evening she made studies for the etching plate the next day. However, in April 1880, Degas abruptly withdrew from the prints journal they had been collaborating on, and without his support, the project folded. Degas' withdrawal piqued Cassatt who had worked hard at preparing a print, _In the Opera Box_, in a large edition of fifty impressions, no doubt destined for the journal. Although Cassatt's warm feelings for Degas were to last her entire life, she never again worked with him as closely as she had over the prints journal. Mathews notes that she ceased executing her theater scenes at this time.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews1994149-70)

Degas was forthright in his views, as was Cassatt.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews1994149-70) They clashed over the [Dreyfus affair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dreyfus_affair "Dreyfus affair") (early in her career she had executed a portrait of the art collector Moyse Dreyfus, a relative of the court-martialled lieutenant at the center of the affair).[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-72)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews1994275-73)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShackelford137-74) Cassatt later expressed satisfaction at the irony of Lousine Havermeyer's 1915 joint exhibition of hers and Degas' work being held in aid of [women's suffrage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage "Women's suffrage"), equally capable of affectionately repeating Degas' antifemale comments as being estranged by them (when viewing her _[Two Women Picking Fruit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two\_Women\_Picking\_Fruit?action=edit&redlink=1 "Two Women Picking Fruit (page does not exist)")_ for the first time, he had commented "No woman has the right to draw like that").[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews1994303,_308-75) From the 1890s onwards their relationship took on a decidedly commercial aspect, as in general had Cassatt's other relations with the Impressionist circle;[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShackelford137-74)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews1994189%E2%80%9390-76) nevertheless they continued to visit each other until Degas died in 1917.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews1994312%E2%80%9313-77)

In 2014, the National Gallery of Art examined their long friendship in its exhibit _Degas/Cassatt_.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-78)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-79) The catalog was written by Kimberly Jones [ISBN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISBN_(identifier) "ISBN (identifier)")[978-3791353647](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:BookSources/978-3791353647 "Special:BookSources/978-3791353647")

## Later life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mary_Cassatt&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Later life")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/Mary_Cassatt_-_The_Child%27s_Bath_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg/330px-Mary_Cassatt_-_The_Child%27s_Bath_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mary_Cassatt_-_The_Child's_Bath_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg)

_[The Child's Bath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Child's\_Bath "The Child's Bath") (The Bath)_ by Mary Cassatt, 1893, oil on canvas, 39 × 26 in., [Art Institute of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Institute_of_Chicago "Art Institute of Chicago")[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-80)

Cassatt's reputation is based on an extensive series of rigorously drawn and tenderly observed paintings and prints on the theme of the mother and child. The earliest dated work on this subject is the [drypoint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drypoint "Drypoint")_Gardner Held by His Mother_ (an impression inscribed "Jan/88" is in the [New York Public Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Public_Library "New York Public Library")),[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews1998182_and_note_on_p._346-81) although she had painted a few earlier works on the theme. Some of these works depict her own relatives, friends, or clients, although in her later years she generally used professional models in compositions that are often reminiscent of [Italian Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Renaissance "Italian Renaissance") depictions of the [Madonna and Child](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madonna_and_Child "Madonna and Child"). After 1900, she concentrated almost exclusively on mother-and-child subjects, such as _[Woman with a Sunflower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woman\_with\_a\_Sunflower "Woman with a Sunflower")_.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKloss1985106-82) Viewers may be surprised to find that despite her focus on portraying mother-child pairs in her portraits, "Cassatt rejected the idea of becoming a wife and mother..."[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-83)

The 1890s were Cassatt's busiest and most creative period. She had matured considerably and became more diplomatic and less blunt in her opinions. She also became a role model for young American artists who sought her advice. Among them was [Lucy A. Bacon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucy_A._Bacon "Lucy A. Bacon"), whom Cassatt introduced to [Camille Pissarro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camille_Pissarro "Camille Pissarro"). Though the Impressionist group disbanded, Cassatt still had contact with some of the members, including Renoir, Monet, and Pissarro.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKown1972155-84)

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/Brooklyn_Museum_-_Mother_and_Child_Before_a_Pool_-_Mary_Cassatt.jpg/250px-Brooklyn_Museum_-_Mother_and_Child_Before_a_Pool_-_Mary_Cassatt.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Brooklyn_Museum_-_Mother_and_Child_Before_a_Pool_-_Mary_Cassatt.jpg)

Mary Cassatt, _Mother and Child Before a Pool_, c.1898. Drypoint and aquatint on laid paper, [Brooklyn Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Museum "Brooklyn Museum")

In 1891, she exhibited a series of highly original colored drypoint and [aquatint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquatint "Aquatint") prints, including _Woman Bathing_ and _[The Coiffure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Coiffure "The Coiffure")_, inspired by the Japanese masters shown in Paris the year before. (See [Japonism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japonism "Japonism")) Cassatt was attracted to the simplicity and clarity of Japanese design and the skillful use of blocks of color. In her interpretation, she used primarily light, delicate pastel colors and avoided black. [Adelyn D. Breeskin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adelyn_Dohme_Breeskin "Adelyn Dohme Breeskin"), the author of two _catalogue raisonnés_ of Cassatt's work, comments that these colored prints, "now stand as her most original contribution... adding a new chapter to the history of graphic arts...technically, as color prints, they have never been surpassed".[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKown1972124%E2%80%93126-85)

Also in 1891, Chicago socialite [Bertha Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertha_Palmer "Bertha Palmer") approached Cassatt to paint a 12' × 58' mural about "Modern Woman" for the Women's Building for the [World's Columbian Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_Columbian_Exposition "World's Columbian Exposition") to be held in 1893. Cassatt completed the project over the next two years while living in France with her mother. The mural was designed as a [triptych](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triptych "Triptych"). The central theme was titled _Young Women Plucking the Fruits of Knowledge or Science_. The left panel was _Young Girls Pursuing Fame_ and the right panel _Arts, Music, Dancing_. The mural displays a community of women apart from their relation to men, as accomplished persons in their own right. Palmer considered Cassatt to be an American treasure and could think of no one better to paint a mural at an exposition that was to do so much to focus the world's attention on the status of women.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-86) Following the world's fair, the mural came into Bertha Palmer's possession, where it remained as late as 1911, but it disappeared after Palmer's death in 1918.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-87) Cassatt made several studies and paintings on themes similar to those in the mural, so it is possible to see her development of those ideas and images.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-88) Cassatt also exhibited other paintings in the Exposition.

As the new century arrived, Cassatt served as an advisor to several major art collectors and stipulated that they eventually donate their purchases to American art museums. In recognition of her contributions to the arts, France awarded her the [Légion d'honneur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9gion_d'honneur "Légion d'honneur") in 1904. Although instrumental in advising American collectors, recognition of her art came more slowly in the United States. Even among her family members back in America, she received little recognition and was totally overshadowed by her famous brother.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKown1972182-89)

Mary Cassatt's brother, [Alexander Cassatt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Cassatt "Alexander Cassatt"), was president of the [Pennsylvania Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Railroad "Pennsylvania Railroad") from 1899 until his death in 1906. She was shaken, as they had been close, but she continued to be very productive in the years leading up to 1910.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews1998281-90) An increasing sentimentality is apparent in her work of the 1900s; her work was popular with the public and the critics, but she was no longer breaking new ground, and her Impressionist colleagues who once provided stimulation and criticism were dying. She was hostile to such new developments in art as [post-Impressionism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-Impressionism "Post-Impressionism"), [Fauvism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fauvism "Fauvism") and [Cubism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubism "Cubism").[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews1998284-91) Two of her works appeared in the [Armory Show of 1913](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armory_Show_of_1913 "Armory Show of 1913"), both images of a mother and child.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-GalleryList-92)

A trip to [Egypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egypt "Egypt") in 1910 impressed Cassatt with the beauty of its ancient art, but was followed by a crisis of creativity; not only had the trip exhausted her, but she declared herself "crushed by the strength of this Art", saying, "I fought against it but it conquered, it is surely the greatest Art the past has left us ... how are my feeble hands to ever paint the effect on me."[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathews1998291-93) Diagnosed with [diabetes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diabetes "Diabetes"), [rheumatism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rheumatism "Rheumatism"), [neuralgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuralgia "Neuralgia"), and [cataracts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cataract "Cataract") in 1911, she did not slow down, but after 1914, she was forced to stop painting as she became almost blind. In 1925 she was featured on 32nd Annual Exhibition of American Art at the [Cincinnati Art Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cincinnati_Art_Museum "Cincinnati Art Museum"), together with [Louise Woodroofe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Woodroofe "Louise Woodroofe"), [Childe Hassam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Childe_Hassam "Childe Hassam") and [Robert Henri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Henri "Robert Henri").[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-94)

Cassatt died on June 14, 1926, at Château de Beaufresne, near Paris, and was buried in the family vault at [Le Mesnil-Théribus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Mesnil-Th%C3%A9ribus "Le Mesnil-Théribus"), France.

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mary_Cassatt&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Legacy")]

*   Mary Cassatt inspired many Canadian women artists who were members of the [Beaver Hall Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaver_Hall_Group "Beaver Hall Group").
*   The [SS _Mary Cassatt_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Liberty_ships:_M "List of Liberty ships: M") was a World War II [Liberty ship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty_ship "Liberty ship"), launched May 16, 1943.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-95)
*   A quartet of young [Juilliard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juilliard "Juilliard") string musicians formed the all-female [Cassatt Quartet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassatt_Quartet "Cassatt Quartet") in 1985, named in honor of the painter.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-96) In 2009, the award-winning group recorded String Quartets Nos. 1–3 (Cassatt String Quartet) by composer [Dan Welcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Welcher "Dan Welcher"); the 3rd quartet on the album was written inspired by the work of Mary Cassatt as well.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-97)
*   In 1966, Cassatt's painting _[The Boating Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Boating\_Party "The Boating Party")_ was reproduced on a US postage stamp. Later she was honored by the [United States Postal Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Postal_Service "United States Postal Service") with a 23-cent [Great Americans series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Americans_series "Great Americans series")[postage stamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postage_stamp "Postage stamp").[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-98)
*   In 1973, Cassatt was inducted into the [National Women's Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Women's_Hall_of_Fame "National Women's Hall of Fame").[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-99)
*   In 2003, four of her paintings – _Young Mother_ (1888), _Children Playing on the Beach_ (1884), _On a Balcony_ (1878/79) and _Child in a Straw Hat_ (c.1886) – were reproduced on the third issue in the American Treasures stamp series.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-100)
*   On May 22, 2009, she was honored by a [Google](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google "Google") Doodle in recognition of her birthday.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-101)
*   Cassatt's paintings have sold for as much as [$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_dollar "United States dollar")4 million, the record price of $4,072,500 being set in 1996 at [Christie's, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christie's "Christie's"), for _[In the Box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In\_the\_Box\_(Cassatt)?action=edit&redlink=1 "In the Box (Cassatt) (page does not exist)")_.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-102)
*   A public garden in the [12th arrondissement of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/12th_arrondissement_of_Paris "12th arrondissement of Paris") is named 'Jardin Mary Cassatt' in her memory.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cassatt#cite_note-103)
